Vote by mail or absentee

Can’t get to your polling place on Election Day? Here is how to vote by mail in Maryland, from the state’s own election office and its laws. Checked October 21, 2026.

Ask for your ballot by

Tuesday, October 27Passed

To have the ballot sent by mail or fax, your request must be in by Tuesday, October 27, 2026. To get a Print-At-Home ballot by e-mailed link, the request must be in by Friday, October 30, 2026. Requests can take about a week to process. (official page)

Send it back by

Tuesday, November 3Passed

Mailed ballots must be postmarked on or before Tuesday, November 3, 2026, and received by the second Friday after the election (Friday, November 13, 2026). Ballots in a drop box or delivered by hand must be in by 8 p.m. on November 3. (official page)

The last day to ask for a ballot by mail has passed. You can still vote in person, early or on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3.You can still vote in person on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3. Early voting in person runs through Thursday, October 29, 2026. When and where to vote early.

Ask for a ballot online, on Maryland’s own site

At school away from home, in Maryland or in another state? What Maryland says about students is under Show more.

Who can vote by mail

No. Any registered voter may vote by mail-in ballot without giving a reason. Maryland uses 'mail-in ballot' and 'absentee ballot' to mean the same thing. You can also join the permanent mail-in ballot list to get a ballot for every future federal and state election. (official page)

How to ask for a ballot

  • Online. Request it online if you have a Maryland driver's license or MVA-issued ID card. Open it (official page)
  • Mail, fax or e-mail. Print, fill out and sign the Mail-in Ballot Application and return it to your local board of elections by mail, fax, in person, or by e-mail with an image of the signed form attached. Your signature is required. Open it (official page)
  • In person. Go to your local board of elections and get a mail-in ballot there. You can also name an agent, using the state's Designation of Agent form, to pick up the ballot for you. (official page)

How to send it back

  • By mail. Mail it in the return envelope, postmarked on or before Election Day. A Print-At-Home ballot goes in your own envelope with your own postage. (official page)
  • Drop box. Any ballot drop box by 8 p.m. on Election Day. Drop box locations come with your ballot. (official page)
  • In person. Deliver it by hand to a voting location or your local board of elections by 8 p.m. on Election Day. You cannot return a voted ballot online, by e-mail or by fax. (official page)

What the envelope needs

Sign the oath that comes with the ballot (do not sign the ballot itself). No witness is needed. If you forget to sign the oath, the local board will try to reach you, and you have until 10 a.m. on Friday, November 13, 2026 to send a signed oath. Some voters must also send ID; that too is due by 10 a.m. on November 13. Anyone who helps you mark your ballot must fill out the Certification of Person Assisting Mail-in Voter, and cannot be a candidate on your ballot, your employer, or an officer or agent of your union. (official page)

Track your ballot

Track your ballot on Maryland’s own site (official page)

Vote early in person instead

Thursday, October 22, 2026 to Thursday, October 29, 2026.

Early voting runs Thursday, October 22 through Thursday, October 29, 2026, from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m., at any early voting center in the county where you live. If you missed the registration deadline, you can register at an early voting center by bringing a document that proves where you live. If you already got a mail-in ballot and then vote in person, you will vote a provisional ballot. (official page)

Students

At school in Maryland, away from home

For college students, the residential address can be your home address or your school address: the one you consider home. If you list a campus address, include your dorm and room number (a PO box is not a residential address). Your mailing address is just where your ballot is sent, so you can, for example, keep your parents' home as your residential address and have the ballot mailed to a campus address or PO box. You can be registered at only one address and vote only once; voting twice is a felony. Voting residency is not the same as residency for in-state tuition, and the state suggests checking whether your choice affects financial aid. (official page)

At school in another state, with Maryland as home

The state's pages do not speak separately to Maryland students at school in another state. Its general rule: your residential address is the one you consider home, and the state can mail ballots anywhere in the world, so you can keep your Maryland registration, set your mailing address to school, and request a mail-in ballot (a student studying abroad should update the mailing address and request one; the ballot can be mailed abroad or downloaded). A student from another state at school in Maryland may stay registered at home or register at the school address, depending on which they consider home; if you register in Maryland, cancel your registration in the other state. (official page)

Military and overseas

Uniformed services voters (and their spouses and dependents) and U.S. citizens living overseas can register and vote in Maryland. A request for a ballot by mail or fax must be received by October 27, 2026, and a request for a ballot by e-mail or online by October 30, 2026. The ballot must be postmarked by November 3 and received by the tenth day after the election. The Federal Write-In Absentee Ballot is a backup. (federal guide)

Maryland in the Federal Voting Assistance Program’s guide

Good to know

  • If you plan to vote in person, the state asks you not to sign up for a mail-in ballot: once one is issued to you, voting in person means a provisional ballot.
  • If you have not received a requested ballot a week before the election, contact your local board of elections. The state also has a mail-in ballot replacement page for 2026.
  • Local boards keep counting mail-in ballots after Election Day and finish on Friday, November 13, 2026.
